clue.text: Not a direct flight coming out of Alsace airstrips

indicators.note: the answer's letters emerge, rearranged, from the two words that follow

explanation.surface: An aircraft takes an indirect route after leaving airfields in the French region of Alsace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flight' looks like air travel, but it is a flight of stairs; 'coming out of' rearranges ALSACE AIRSTRIPS.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight is a set of steps, and a helical one winds round rather than going straight up.

clue.text: French novelist climbing in tree

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means the novelist's name is written from bottom to top

parts.note: Albert Camus wrote The Outsider and The Plague

explanation.surface: A writer from France is up a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'climbing' turns CAMUS upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a shrub or small tree with red fruit clusters, used as a spice.

clue.text: Gauche line sadly taken on say, worker

indicators.note: sadly signals the word line is rendered badly, its letters jumbled

parts.note: say means for example, abbreviated EG
a worker is an ant, as in a worker ant

explanation.surface: An awkward line of verse, perhaps penned by a labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges LINE as INEL; 'taken on' joins EG and ANT behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone clumsy and lacking grace or polish.

clue.text: Singer in the nude, get her off!

indicators.note: off says the words get her are taken away from the longer word

parts.note: to be 'in the altogether' is a jokey idiom for being naked, so the altogether is the nude

explanation.surface: A heckler at a strip show yells for a naked singer to be removed from the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get her off!' sounds like a heckle, but 'off' removes the letters GETHER from the end of the idiom for nudity.
explanation.definitionFit: A voice part below soprano, and so a vocalist who sings it.

clue.text: "Observer" featuring the inventor of gamesmanship briefly

indicators.note: briefly says his name is shortened, the first name cut down to its initial

parts.note: Stephen Potter's 1947 book coined the word gamesmanship for winning by psychological ploys

explanation.surface: The Observer newspaper runs a piece by the man who invented gamesmanship.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Potter, the British humorist, is written S. Potter in short, and the two run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who watches out for and notes things, such as a trainspotter or aircraft lookout.

clue.text: Delegates behind arresting banner

indicators.note: arresting means holding or catching, so the bottom word holds the banner word inside it

parts.note: behind is the buttocks, in American slang an ass
a banner is a sign carrying a message

explanation.surface: Conference delegates sit behind a striking banner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delegates' looks like a noun, people sent to a conference, but it is a verb: hands out tasks. 'behind' is slang for the bottom, not a position.
explanation.definitionFit: To delegate a task is to hand it on, or allot it, to someone else.

clue.text: Editing a work on origin of dada movement

parts.note: on means concerning, the Latin-derived re

indicators.note: the origin of a word is its opening letter, so dada gives its first letter only

parts.note: movement is motion or action

explanation.surface: An editor works on a text about the beginnings of the Dada art movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dada movement' looks like the art movement; 'origin of' takes only its D, and 'movement' is ACTION.
explanation.definitionFit: Redaction is the preparing of a text for publication by revising it.

clue.text: Some maniac cracked in capital

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A lunatic has a breakdown in a major city.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft gave 'in capital' as the definition, but 'in' is a link word: the answer means 'capital', not 'in capital'.
explanation.definitionFit: The city is the seat of government of Ghana.

clue.text: Hears? Nope, when sporting these

indicators.note: sporting means playing about, so the letters of hears and nope frolic into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone wearing headphones cannot hear what is said to them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sporting' rearranges HEARS NOPE; the whole clue also describes the answer, as headphones cut out sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearing a headset blocks outside speech, so the wearer misses what is said.

clue.text: Rattle perhaps, in car

explanation.surface: A rattle can be heard inside a motor.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Simon Rattle is a British conductor; the Austin Maestro was a British family car of the 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: A great conductor is given this title of master; also a model of hatchback from British Leyland.

clue.text: Vehicle contest date that is rejected

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the whole run of pieces is read backwards

parts.note: a contest of speed is a race

explanation.surface: An application for a contest date has been turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that' is a link; 'rejected' turns RACE+D+IS backwards as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-wheeled passenger carriage attached alongside a motorcycle.

clue.text: School managed without pressure

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the pressure letter drops out

parts.note: to manage a difficulty is to cope with it
P is the physics symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: A school got by without any stress.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for coeducational, a mixed school taking both boys and girls.

clue.text: Wise person includes time to teach diligence?

indicators.note: includes means the wise person holds the time letter inside

parts.note: a sage is a wise man
to teach someone a skill is to coach them

explanation.surface: A wise teacher takes time to instil hard work in pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'diligence' looks like hard work, but a diligence was a public horse-drawn coach in France.
explanation.definitionFit: A diligence was a horse-drawn public carriage running on a fixed route between towns.

clue.text: Two of us (according to eastenders) wander about

indicators.note: London East Enders drop their aitches, so the H is lost

parts.note: a pair of people can be named as me and her

explanation.surface: Two characters from the TV soap stroll aimlessly around Albert Square.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a BBC soap set in East London, whose Cockney speakers drop H, so 'me and her' becomes ME AND 'ER.
explanation.definitionFit: To move about along a winding course without any set purpose.

clue.text: Handles detractors around n Ireland

indicators.note: around means the mockers word goes round the Irish letters

parts.note: detractors who ridicule are mockers
NI is the abbreviation for Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Critics manhandle people around Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handles' looks like a verb, but it is slang for names.
explanation.definitionFit: A handle is slang for a name or nickname, as in a CB radio call sign.

clue.text: Brave actions going wrong in democratic party

indicators.note: in puts the mistake word inside the pair of letters around it

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for Democratic, as in US politics
a do is an informal word for a party
erring means making a mistake

explanation.surface: Bold moves are failing within the Democratic Party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going wrong' looks like the anagram signal, but it is a synonym in its own right, and 'party' is the British informal word for a social do.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroic, daring exploits, from a Middle English phrase meaning daring to do.

clue.text: Continues to travel in Laos moving around south

indicators.note: around means the jumbled letters go round the compass letter
moving tells the solver to shift the letters of in and Laos into a fresh order

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A traveller keeps going through Laos, heading south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' rearranges the letters of 'in Laos' to SAILON, and 'around' wraps that round the south letter. Laos looks like the traveller's destination, but it only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat that proceeds on its voyage keeps going under canvas.

clue.text: Alert child good with alluring music

parts.note: an alert or alarm is a siren
a son is a male child

explanation.surface: An observant, well-behaved youngster is drawn to seductive tunes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alert' looks like an adjective but is the noun, an alarm.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Sirens' singing lured sailors to wreck, so the phrase means a tempting appeal.

clue.text: Nag's head, for instance, accommodates awfully true characters

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
accommodates means holds inside, so the scrambled word sits within the other piece

parts.note: as means for instance, as in sports such as tennis

indicators.note: awfully means badly, so the letters of true are jumbled

explanation.surface: A pub called the Nag's Head houses some very honest regulars.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nag's Head is a common British pub name, which makes 'head' read as part of a name; 'awfully' rearranges the letters of true, giving TURE.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's character is their disposition or temperament.

clue.text: Two notes from awkward customer

explanation.surface: Two banknotes come from a difficult client.
explanation.walkthrough: In tonic sol-fa, so (or sol) is a note, so a note plus another note reads as the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally one sol-fa note and then the same again; also a euphemism for an unpleasant person.

clue.text: Could be jokers catching a number with unfounded stories

indicators.note: catching means the cards word holds the article and number inside it

parts.note: jokers are playing cards, so they are an example of the plural
N is the mathematical symbol for any number

explanation.surface: Pranksters spreading rumours about a figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be' signals that jokers are an example of what is meant; 'catching' puts AN inside CARDS.
explanation.definitionFit: A canard is a false rumour or hoax, from the French for duck.

clue.text: Hairstyle for the team?

parts.note: read as a trim given to a boat's rowers, it names a short, bristly haircut

explanation.definitionFit: A very short, flat-topped cut, once worn by college rowing crews.

clue.text: Engineer vacates pit entrances

indicators.note: to engineer is to contrive or construct, so these letters are rebuilt

explanation.surface: A mining engineer leaves the pit by its entrances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entrances' looks like doorways, but it is the verb, to enchant; 'Engineer' rearranges VACATES PIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance someone is to delight and hold them spellbound.

clue.text: Measure of freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A unit of size for a river fish.
explanation.definitionFit: An old unit of length, five and a half yards, also called a rod or pole; and a spiny-finned river species.

clue.text: Girl over in us restaurant getting bottom pinched

indicators.note: over means turned back, so the shortened word is read in reverse
the bottom, the last letter, is pinched, that is stolen, from the eatery

parts.note: a diner is a cheap roadside eatery in the United States

explanation.surface: A young woman in an American cafe is groped from behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting bottom pinched' sounds like harassment, but removes the last letter R; 'over' then reverses DINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, as in the children's author Enid Blyton.

clue.text: A house in Germany you and I left empty

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'A house in Germany you and I left empty' (5): D + WE + LT builds the whole answer, leaving 'A house' as the definition, which is a noun and cannot stand for the past tense verb; the defining word appears garbled (likely 'Housed') and no source gives the printed clue.
annotationWithheld.clue: A house in Germany you and I left empty

clue.text: Gen's pregnant. Al's gone missing!

indicators.note: gone missing says those letters disappear from the pregnancy phrase

parts.note: a mare carrying young is said to be in foal
Al is a man's name, shortened from Alan or Albert

explanation.surface: Gossip that a woman is expecting while her partner has disappeared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gen' looks like a woman's name, but it is British slang for information; 'gone missing' removes AL from IN FOAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal shortenings meaning facts or intelligence.

clue.text: Stop without proper gear on the warpath?

indicators.note: without means outside, so the stopping word goes round the other letters

parts.note: to stop is to end

indicators.note: proper is read as put into proper order, so the letters of gear are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone stopped for lacking the right kit goes into a fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' surrounds RAGE (the letters of GEAR rearranged, signalled by 'proper') with END. 'proper' is an unusual anagram signal; the question mark marks the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is furious is ready to fight, like a warrior setting out to attack.

clue.text: Calm prisoner alone

parts.note: a con is a convict, a prisoner
sole means single, the only one

explanation.surface: A prisoner in solitary confinement stays calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Calm' looks like an adjective, but it is the verb: to soothe.
explanation.definitionFit: To comfort someone in distress is to soothe them.

clue.text: Approach training with careful consideration

parts.note: to school someone is to train them
describing something done with reflection, as in a man of thought

explanation.surface: A method of teaching that involves deep reflection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Approach' is a noun here, a particular way of looking at things.
explanation.definitionFit: A shared set of ideas held by a group of thinkers is a way of approaching a subject.
